lesson_title: Stalin's terror: purges, show trials and gulag
claim: Nikolai Bukharin, once described by Lenin as 'the golden boy of the revolution.'
issue: Lenin never used the phrase 'golden boy of the revolution' in his Testament or in any verified primary source. Lenin's Testament (1922–23) calls Bukharin 'not only a most valuable and major theorist of the Party' but also 'rightly considered the favourite of the whole Party' and criticises his scholastic grasp of dialectics. 'Golden boy of the revolution' is a popular secondary paraphrase found in journalism, not Lenin's words. Attributing it as Lenin's description is a misattribution.
correction: Replace with Lenin's actual Testament wording: Bukharin was described by Lenin as 'the favourite of the whole Party' and 'the most valuable and biggest theoretician of the party', though Lenin also criticised his theoretical weaknesses. Do not attribute 'golden boy of the revolution' to Lenin.
source: Lenin's Testament (Letter to the Congress, Dec 1922–Jan 1923): https://www.marxists.org/archive/lenin/works/1922/dec/testamnt/congress.htm

claim: The Battle of Stalingrad lasted from August 1942 to February 1943 ... German forces under Field Marshal Paulus drove deep into the city
issue: Paulus was not a Field Marshal during the Battle of Stalingrad. He held the rank of Generaloberst (Colonel-General) throughout the fighting. Hitler promoted him to Generalfeldmarschall (Field Marshal) on 31 January 1943 — the very day Paulus surrendered — as a signal that no German Field Marshal should surrender. The lesson's use of 'Field Marshal Paulus' in the context of driving into the city implies he held this rank during the battle, which is misleading.
correction: Refer to him as 'General Paulus' (or 'Generaloberst Paulus') during the battle. His promotion to Field Marshal came only on the day of his surrender (31 January 1943). The surrender paragraph is separately accurate in calling him 'Paulus' without a title.

lesson_title: The Home Front in the Second World War
claim: The Coventry raid of 14 November 1940, in which over 500 bombers dropped incendiary and high-explosive bombs, destroyed the medieval city centre and killed approximately 554 people.
issue: The figure of 554 does not appear in standard scholarly sources for this raid. The most widely cited figure in authoritative sources (Wikipedia, GCHQ, Historic Coventry, Coventry City Council) is approximately 568 killed. The International Churchill Society gives 507. No standard reference gives 554. The bomber figure of 'over 500' is within the range of sources (515–552) and is acceptable.
correction: Replace '554' with 'approximately 568' (the most cited figure in standard historical references) or use 'approximately 500–570' to reflect the range across sources. Note that exact figures were never confirmed and differ across sources.
source: Wikipedia Coventry Blitz: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry_Blitz; GCHQ: https://www.gchq.gov.uk/information/the-bombing-of-coventry-in-wwii; Historic Coventry: https://www.historiccoventry.co.uk/blitz/blitz.php?pg=stats

claim: Labour won 393 seats with 48 per cent of the vote [in 1945]
issue: The 393 seats figure is correct. However, Labour's vote share in the 1945 election was approximately 47.7% (House of Commons Library) or 48.3% depending on source — not a clean '48 per cent'. More precisely, standard academic sources give 47.7% (UK Parliament/House of Commons Library). Stating '48 per cent' slightly overstates the share, though it is a rounding issue rather than a fabrication. This claim appears in lesson 4 (Post-war Britain) not lesson 1, but is flagged here as the most accurate lesson_id for the content.
correction: Change '48 per cent' to 'approximately 48 per cent' or more precisely '47.7 per cent'. The 393 seats figure is correct.
source: House of Commons Library UK Election Statistics 1918–2023: https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-7529/; Wikipedia 1945 election: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1945_United_Kingdom_general_election

claim: Labour won 393 seats with 48 per cent of the vote.
issue: The 393 seats figure is correct. Labour's actual vote share in 1945 was approximately 47.7% per the House of Commons Library, not a clean 48%. While minor, stating '48 per cent' is a rounding that slightly overstates Labour's share. Some sources give slightly different figures depending on how turnout and spoiled ballots are handled, but no authoritative source gives a clean 48.0%.
correction: Change to 'approximately 48 per cent' or more accurately '47.7 per cent'. The seat count of 393 is correct.

claim: The Beatles, formed in Liverpool and achieving their first UK number one in 1963 with 'From Me to You'
issue: This is defensible but contested. 'From Me to You' (April 1963) was the first Beatles single to reach No. 1 on the Record Retailer chart (now the Official UK Singles Chart). However, 'Please Please Me' (January 1963) reached No. 1 on multiple other contemporary charts (NME, Melody Maker, Disc). The lesson's phrasing is consistent with the modern Official Charts Company position, which retrospectively recognises 'From Me to You' as the first No. 1. This is not an error but worth noting the chart complexity if precision is needed.
correction: The claim is acceptable per Official Charts Company. If precision is desired, add a qualifier: 'achieving their first UK number one on the official chart in 1963 with "From Me to You"' — noting that 'Please Please Me' topped several other contemporary charts.
